**Do the orbits differ from F9?** No. Every parameter matches F9 to at least four significant figures. The fit started at 193.5 d and 89.2 d and ended at 189.3 d and 91.8 d. The inner eccentricity again lands on exactly 0.450, the value the critic said may be the fitter's starting value. Since F9 repeats the F2 solution that failed on orbital match, F15 is the same refuted configuration under a new ID.

**Narrower check (F16, ±2%):** I also kept both periods within 2% of the H8 starting values to see whether the data support a separate 193.5 d / 89.2 d solution. They don't. Both periods ran to the edge of the allowed range on the side toward F9: outer 189.81 d and inner 90.98 d, both flagged as stuck on the bound. Scatter rose to 2.81 m/s (limit 3.77 m/s), and BIC rose to 371.3, which is 19.3 worse than F15/F9 and so decisive. The best fit in the ledger stays F15/F9, and the 193.5 d peak doesn't lead to a better two-planet orbit.

**Residual signals (F15):** the strongest residual peak is 1.60 d, with a false-alarm probability of 0.46 against the 1% threshold. The next peaks are 2.56 d (0.73), 2.48 d (0.74), 1.65 d (0.79), 5.11 d (0.89) and 8.26 d (0.91). Several are flagged as harmonics of each other, which looks like noise. No unexplained signal is left, and nothing points to a third planet.

**Bottom line:** H8 explains the data statistically, but it gives the same orbits as F9/F2, which already failed the orbital-match check. It is not a new candidate and shouldn't be submitted. A different solution will probably need the other eccentricity mode the critic suggested (eccentric outer planet, near-circular inner one), or follow-up points at the epochs where the competing solutions differ most. That decision is yours.
